01-c1.claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., yet the majority of public high schools in the United States still begin before that.

sources.title: School Start Times for Adolescents
sources.snippet: The American Academy of Pediatrics urges middle and high schools to aim for starting times no earlier than 8:30 a.m.

sources.title: Start Time for U.S. Public High Schools

01-c3.claim: The consequence is not subtle: pushing start times later has been shown to increase how long students sleep, and districts that made the change saw fewer car crashes among teen drivers.

sources.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
sources.snippet: A one-hour delay increased adolescent sleep and teen-driver crash rates fell 16.5% afterward, while rates elsewhere in the state rose 7.8%.

sources.title: School Start Times and Teenage Driver Motor Vehicle Crashes
sources.snippet: Later high-school start times above 8:30 a.m. appeared associated with lower adolescent driver crash rates, though further research was needed.

sources.title: School Start Times and Teenage Driver Motor Vehicle Crashes
sources.snippet: NHTSA reports research showing reduced teen-driver motor-vehicle crashes when high-school start times are delayed.

sources.title: Drowsy driving and teen motor vehicle crashes: Impact of changing school start times
sources.snippet: “CONCLUSIONS: Healthy school start times are important for adolescent health and safety, with study findings highlighting the downstream effects of increased sleep duration following a 70-min delay in secondary school start times on adolescent drowsy driving and teen MVC rates”
sources.quote: CONCLUSIONS: Healthy school start times are important for adolescent health and safety, with study findings highlighting the downstream effects of increased sleep duration following a 70-min delay in secondary school start times on adolescent drowsy driving and teen MVC rates

sources.title: School Start Times for Adolescents
sources.snippet: A district delaying start times by one hour found students slept 12 to 30 minutes more nightly, with adequate sleepers increasing from 37% to 50%.

01-c4.claim: Studies show that this sleep debt is the primary driver of the adolescent mental health crisis, and experts agree that smartphones have made it worse.

sources.quote: The methodological quality of the studies was generally poor

sources.snippet: Among 10,588 adolescents, acquiring a smartphone was associated with greater odds of clinical-level psychopathology and insufficient sleep after adjustment for baseline factors.

sources.title: Impact of mobile phones and wireless devices use on children and adolescents’ mental health: a systematic review
sources.snippet: The review finds associations between mobile-device use and mental-health outcomes but says more longitudinal and mechanistic research is needed to clarify causality and the role of sleep.

sources.title: Mental Health and Suicide Risks | Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS)

sources.snippet: The study describes rising depressive symptoms and notes that major-depression prevalence among adolescent females doubled from 11.4% to 23.4% between 2009 and 2019.

sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

sources.quote: work from home 5 days a week) encounter comparable and diminished prospects for promotion and salary increases

03-c1.claim: Johannes Gutenberg introduced movable-type printing to Europe around 1450, and within fifty years printing presses were operating in more than two hundred European cities.

sources.title: Printing

sources.quote: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg introduced the first movable-type printing system in Europe

sources.title: Information technology and economic change: The impact of the printing press

sources.title: Printing

sources.quote: By 1500 printing offizins had emerged at around 250 locations

sources.title: Information technology and economic change: The impact of the printing press

sources.title: Charting the “Rise of the West”: Manuscripts and Printed Books in Europe, A Long-Term Perspective from the Sixth through Eighteenth Centuries
sources.snippet: The article attributes rising European book production after the fifteenth century partly to lower book prices and higher literacy, with laypeople increasingly driving demand.

sources.title: The great divergence and the economics of printing

sources.snippet: The field is characterized by small average effects that vary between studies, with outcomes moderated by user characteristics, content, and how social media is used.

sources.title: Media Effects: Advances in Theory and Research

sources.title: Adolescent social media use and mental health in the Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) Study

sources.title: Associations Between Time Spent Using Social Media and Internalizing and Externalizing Problems Among US Youth

08-c1.claim: Ramirez and Doyle (2024) found that students who received AI-generated feedback improved their essay scores by 23 percent over a single semester, a larger effect than any human intervention has produced.

sources.title: A gut microbiome tactile teaching tool and guided-inquiry activity promotes student learning
sources.snippet: The article reports a guided-inquiry teaching activity and cites studies involving Ramirez and Doyle, but it does not report AI-generated essay feedback or a 23 percent improvement.

sources.title: A gut microbiome tactile teaching tool and guided-inquiry activity promotes student learning
sources.snippet: The study describes pre- and post-assessment scores for a biology teaching activity, not AI-generated feedback on student essays.

sources.title: International education reform: A review of research and policy
sources.snippet: The document discusses international education policy and cites older work by Ramirez and other authors, with no evidence of the claimed 2024 AI-feedback study.

08-c2.claim: Their sample was large and the effect held across grade levels, so the usual complaints about small studies do not apply here.

sources.title: Automated feedback and writing: a multi-level meta-analysis of effects on students’ performance
sources.snippet: The meta-analysis included 20 studies with 2,828 participants, indicating a broader evidence base but not a single large study spanning all grade levels.

sources.title: A systematic review of AI-based automated written feedback research
sources.snippet: The review reports varied participants, sample sizes, durations, genres, and research methods across automated written-feedback studies.

sources.title: Automated Essay Scoring in Middle School Writing: Understanding Key Predictors of Students’ Growth and Comparing Artificial Intelligence- and Teacher-Generated Scores and Feedback
sources.snippet: The study analyzes 3,233 seventh- and eighth-grade students, limiting its reported grade-level evidence to middle school.

sources.title: Comparing the quality of human and ChatGPT feedback of students’ writing
sources.snippet: The study compares 200 human-generated and 200 AI-generated feedback items on secondary student essays and examines differences by essay quality and learner status.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of Automated Writing Evaluation Feedback: Validity, Effects and Students’ Engagement
sources.snippet: This 2024 systematic review examines evidence on automated-writing feedback’s validity, effects, engagement, and student outcomes rather than confirming a uniform effect across grade levels.

sources.title: Comparing GPT and human raters in essay assessment: Variability, bias, and the potential of LLM-based scoring
sources.snippet: This study compares GPT-based automated essay scoring with 20 human raters across 181 university-level second-language essays and four analytic criteria.

08-c4.claim: Every English teacher I know is quietly worried that AI will grade essays better than they do, and the research says they are right to worry.

sources.title: Examining the responsible use of zero-shot AI approaches to scoring essays
sources.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
sources.snippet: AI scores averaged 0.9 points below human ratings, matched them about 30% of the time, and came within one point 77% of the time.

sources.title: Can AI provide useful holistic essay scoring?
sources.snippet: AI-human agreement was moderate to fair, and the study concludes that humans should score summative assessments compared with untrained language models.

sources.title: Grading the Graders: Comparing Generative AI and Human Assessment in Essay Evaluation
sources.snippet: The study found that AI and human instructors differed in how they scored essays using the same rubric, while AI may support grading processes.

sources.title: Large language models and automated essay scoring of English language learner writing: Insights into validity and reliability
sources.snippet: Researchers evaluated four language models against two human raters to examine the validity and reliability of automated scoring for English-language learners.
